title: Lifting the anathemas (1965)
hook: Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras lift the mutual excommunications from the old split between East and West

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vatican II, and a pope who wanted fresh air. Your line: open the windows.

Two churches, one statement, read aloud on the same day in two cities. In Rome, at the end of the council, before the bishops. In Istanbul, the old Constantinople, in the patriarch's church. It's about something that happened long before anyone in either room was born. At the time of the great split between the Christian East and West, envoys from Rome and the patriarch in Constantinople had pronounced sentences of excommunication on each other. Those sentences sat on the record ever since, like a door slammed and never reopened. Now Pope Paul the Sixth and Patriarch Athenagoras agree to lift them.

An anathema is a solemn curse or ban, a sentence that puts someone outside the church. The word is in the New Testament. When Paul writes to the Galatians about anyone who preaches a different gospel, the King James Bible gives it as "let him be accursed." Strong words, meant for serious cases. The usual story of the old split: Envoys from Rome, in Constantinople, laid a document of excommunication on the altar of the great church there, and walked out. The patriarch and his synod answered with excommunications of their own. The quarrel had many roots, theology, authority, language, politics, and those sentences became a symbol of all of it. Then two men acted. Paul and Athenagoras had already met and embraced in Jerusalem. Now, in a joint declaration, they regretted the offensive words and hurtful actions of that time, and asked that the sentences be removed from memory and from the midst of the church, consigned to oblivion. What it didn't do matters too. It didn't restore full communion. The two churches still don't celebrate the Eucharist together, and their dialogue continues, patiently, on both sides. The declaration itself says the gesture isn't enough to end the differences. It was a start. Jesus put the order plainly, in the King James Bible: "Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift." The story goes that the old sentence from Rome was laid on an altar. The undoing began when both sides laid it aside.

Let one medium-sized old grudge come to mind: a cousin, an old friend, a former boss. Notice how long you've kept it on the record and what it costs to keep it there, and ask what lifting the sentence would mean, even if nothing else changes yet. If you pray, bring Jesus's words about leaving the gift at the altar.
anathema. Greek for a solemn curse, the old sentences of excommunication that Pope Paul the Sixth and Patriarch Athenagoras set aside between Rome and Constantinople.
Your line: nine hundred years undone. Undone, but not yet one. Day nine hundred sixty-four, complete.

howItsDone: Delegations from Rome and from the patriarchate in Istanbul now visit each other on their churches' patronal feast days, and official dialogue between the two churches continues.

fork.setup: you're a church leader. an old sentence against another church has sat on the record for a very long time. both sides still disagree on real things. what do you do?
options: leave it; nothing can be done until every question is settled.
lift the old sentence together, and keep talking about the rest.
issue a new sentence to match.
fork.reveal: Paul and Athenagoras lifted the sentences together and said the gesture was not enough on its own. the deeper questions are still being worked through.

what a scholar hears: the old sentences fell on particular men, the envoys and the patriarch, not on whole churches; the joint declaration asked that they be removed from memory, a gesture its signers said was not enough on its own.

chat.says: So in 1965 the Catholic and Orthodox churches became one church again?
options: Not yet. They lifted the old excommunications, but still don't share the Eucharist; the dialogue goes on.
Yes. Lifting the old sentences restored full communion, so now they share the Eucharist.
No. The statement blamed the other side for the split and asked them to apologize first.
chat.meaning: The joint declaration regretted the old words and set the sentences aside, but it didn't restore full communion. The two churches' dialogue continues.

Constantinople.meaning: the old name of Istanbul, the patriarch's city

Athenagoras.meaning: the patriarch of Constantinople who met Pope Paul the Sixth

excommunication.meaning: a sentence shutting someone out of the church's communion

Eucharist.meaning: the shared bread and cup of communion
